transcript.text: Before coding, describe the algorithm you would try for the longest common substring of ABABC and BABCA. What do the pointers or states represent?
I would use two pointers, one at the start of each string. If the characters match, I extend the current substring. Otherwise, I reset the count and move both pointers forward.
How would you handle cases where the characters do not match while using your two-pointer approach?
My method only examines positions where both pointers have advanced equally. It could miss a common substring starting at different offsets, such as BABC in the example.
What adjustments could you make to your two-pointer method to ensure it captures common substrings that start at different offsets in the two strings?

I could use a 2D table. dp[i][j] is the length of the common substring ending at the i-th character of s1 and j-th character of s2. When they match, use dp[i-1][j-1]+1; otherwise reset to zero. Track the maximum.
How would you adapt your 2D table approach to handle the integer arrays [1,2,3,2,1] and [3,2,1,4,7] for finding the longest shared contiguous run?

The reusable principle is to represent a problem using states defined by the endpoints of two sequences. Matching elements extend a contiguous run; mismatches break it. Considering every pair of endpoints avoids missing shifted alignments.
How would you specifically implement the idea of using states defined by the endpoints of two sequences to find the longest shared contiguous run in the integer arrays [1,2,3,2,1] and [3,2,1,4,7]?

For two integer arrays, I can use the same dp[i][j] as the length of the common contiguous subarray ending at those indices. Equal integers extend the diagonal by one, unequal integers reset it to zero. I track the largest value.
What specific adjustments would you make to your approach if the integer arrays contained negative numbers or zeros, and how would that affect your dp table calculations?
